newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong's 10-year EF note makes noteworthy debut.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's 10-year EF note makes noteworthy debut.

text.p: The Hong Kong Exchange Fund Note market made a notable entrance into the ranks of the world's most developed government bond markets with its debut 10-year government bond, traders and analysts said Monday.

"With this tender, the Hong Kong government capital market is a fully mature market comparable to the Australian, French of German markets," said Andrew Fung, head of capital markets, Asia, at Commonwealth Bank of Australia in Hong Kong.
"In most of the mature markets, the liquid yield curve is only extended to 10 years. Only the U.S. market is exceptional with the 30-year liquid benchmark," he added.
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) on Monday sold HK$500 million in 7.37 percent bonds due 2006 at an average accepted yield of 7.57 percent.
The issue was a 13.5 times oversubscribed with HK$7.26 billion applied for, a record oversubscription for a Hong Kong note tender.
Traders said the huge demand suggested that the 10-year issue attracted institutional investors as well as market makers in Exchange Fund Notes (EFN).

"I suspect that some of the pension funds, some of the semi-government bodies like the Housing Society and some of the treasury sections of Hong Kong government bodies participated in the issue," said an EFN trader at a U.S. bank here.
Fung said the longer tenor likely attracted the type of institutional investors that might shun five-year or even seven-year paper.
"I think that some insurance companies came into this tender as this is the first time that those investors that have very long-term liabilities have been offered a very liquid instrument," he said.
Traders said the issue rallied almost immediately after launch to yield 7.55 percent.
The issue priced to yield 93 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries. Prior to the tender, the notes were trading at a spread of 96-97 basis points in the grey market, traders said.
They said further tightening is possible.

"We will probably see prices firming from here and I think that we also will probably see the spread against the swap settle very much like the five year," said Anita Fung, manager of Hong Kong domestic markets at HSBC Markets.
At present, the market for 10-year swaps is illiquid and the bid-ask spread can be about eight basis points versus three basis points in the five- to seven-years sector, she said.
Commonwealth Bank of Australia's Fung said he wouldn't be surprised to see the 10-year note's spread narrow to 85 basis points over Treasuries.

He noted that the entire Hong Kong government bond yield curve has been tightening versus Treasuries because of consistent capital flows into the territory, a strong Hong Kong dollar exchange value and a buoyant local stock market.

Traders said they expected liquidity in the new benchmark issue to be ample, given market-makers' responsibility to provide price quotes at all times. Turnover is unlikely to be as high as for three- and five-year paper, however.

The 10-year notes will be offered on a quarterly basis. Some traders have charged that tendering new notes four times a year could flood the market with unwanted paper, steepening the yield curve at the long end.
But others said such worries were misplaced.
"This morning's results show that there is a substantial demand for 10-year paper by some private investors, so the market is not totally in the hands of market-makers," said the U.S. bank trader.
